Nursing Program — Key Updates & Action Items
Curriculum Review
Spring 2026: faculty began a thorough review of the AS Nursing curriculum at both the program and course level. Improvements based on faculty expertise and MOHHS nurse input are under review by the curriculum committee.
New Faculty Hired
Fall 2025: CMI hired a new nursing faculty member with a PhD in Hospital Administration, MBA in Health Care Services, and MSc in Nursing — a key step toward programmatic accreditation.
International Students
Fall 2025 enrolled nursing majors included 9 students from the FSM and 2 from the Philippines — growing the international pipeline into RMI healthcare.
Accreditation Pathway
CMI expects to submit its initial application to ASEN (programmatic accreditor for associate-level nursing programs) by April 2026, beginning the candidacy process toward full accreditation.
CNA & LPN Programs
CMI met with MOHHS stakeholders on the RMI nursing shortage. Plans developed for a Certified Nursing Assistant (CNA) program in high schools and a Licensed Practical Nurse (LPN) certificate — both as stepping stones to the ASN degree.
CHOW Completion
CHOW students completing their program in Spring 2026 will enroll in the Certificate of Completion in Outer Atoll Health Assistant (CC-OAHA).

Maritime Milestone
May 2025: first graduates of CC-RFPNW and CC-RFPERW. 100% entered the workforce — featured in ACCJC white paper.
Sea-Time Guidance
Guided 22 students through required sea-time. Participated in GIZ Low Carbon Sea Transport Workshop.
International Reach
Maritime instructors presented at the FFA 7th Maritime College Seminar in the Solomon Islands.
ABE & Outer Centers — Key Data
Uliga (Main)
ABE program continues to be CMI's largest community-serving department with 300+ learners. Level 5 practicum in bookkeeping, automotive, woodworking, and clothing & textiles. Administers both U.S. HiSET and RMI HiSET.
Kwajalein Campus
Fall 2025: 101 ABE students registered, 87 regularly attending. Summer Boot Camp graduated 35 participants — including 3 women in Automotive and Welding.
Wotje Center (23 Students)
May 2025: 3 students graduated with Associate degrees in Elementary Education — the highest number of college graduates from Wotje yet.
Jaluit Center (44 Students)
Steady increases in enrollment at both college and ABE levels thanks to targeted outreach in the atoll community.
Arrak Campus
New TVET building opened April 15, 2026 (World Bank funded). Carpentry students building drinking-water catchment systems for Laura Elementary, Laura High School, and Woja Elementary.
Expansion
New sub-centers in Likiep and Ejit in development — placement testing completed and community partnerships established.

📊

How to read this section

Amounts are summarized directly from the attached GL detail. Activity is debit + credit volume, while Net is debit minus credit. The report avoids listing individual payroll/person-level detail and focuses on fund, GL, department, month, and transaction-source summaries.

Financial Report Filters
Multi-select enabled: leave a list blank to include all values. Use Ctrl/Cmd-click or Shift-click to select more than one item.
Privacy note: Vendor / Name filtering is hidden because the GL Name column can contain individual student or employee names. Use Department, Fund, Object, FABS, PIN/Program, Quarter, Month, Date Range, and Amount Range for analysis instead.
Assumptions: Quarter and Month are derived from the PostTo date. Object means GL code plus GL Title. The Vendor / Name filter is hidden for privacy because the Name column may contain individual names. PIN is mapped to the Program column because the file has no field named PIN. FABS means rows where the GL record text contains FABS. Amount Range filters on row activity, calculated as Debit + Credit. Multi-select fields use exact selected values; no selection in a list means all values.

Analysis Narrative
Completed-year trend
FY2021-FY2025 shows a structural shift from surplus to deficit. Revenue increased by $446,045.02 (4.42%) from FY2021 to FY2025, while expenditures increased by $2,119,133.80 (21.90%). Net position changed by ($1,673,088.78) over the same period.
Peak and low points
FY2022 was the strongest year in the workbook. It had the highest revenue at $12,679,610.26 and the highest surplus at $1,800,456.28. FY2023 had the highest expenditures at $13,103,815.54 and the largest deficit at ($1,646,905.71).
FY2025 movement
FY2025 revenue and expenses both decreased from FY2024, but revenue fell faster. Revenue decreased by $994,784.34 (8.63%), expenditures decreased by $640,646.99 (5.15%), and the net position worsened by $354,137.35 to a ($1,259,975.22) deficit.
Revenue pressure
RMI Subsidy declined across completed years. RMI Subsidy moved from $3,961,222.00 in FY2021 to $3,317,857.00 in FY2025, a change of ($643,365.00) (-16.24%). Tuition & Fees remained the largest FY2026 revenue category at $2,938,566.00, or 48.19% of FY2026 revenue.
Cost drivers
Personnel-related categories are the main expenditure drivers. Salaries & Wages increased by $1,665,752.15 (41.96%) from FY2021 to FY2025, and Benefits increased by $633,749.38 (45.67%). In FY2026, Salaries & Wages represent 55.29% of recorded expenditures.

Institutional Self Evaluation Report (ISER) must be submitted to ACCJC. This is CMI's comprehensive accreditation self-study, covering all four standards areas.
About ACCJC
The Accrediting Commission for Community and Junior Colleges (ACCJC) is CMI's regional accreditor. ACCJC accreditation affirms that CMI meets established standards of quality and is authorized to award degrees and certificates recognized by U.S. federal and state agencies.
Why it matters: Accreditation is required for students to access federal financial aid, for CMI's degrees to be recognized by employers and transfer institutions, and for the college to remain eligible for federal grant programs including Title IV.
📌

Warning vs. Probation

Warning is the first level of sanction. If CMI fails to meet the November 1 deadline, ACCJC could escalate to Probation or Show Cause — a serious outcome that could affect student aid eligibility.

✅

Midterm Accepted

ACCJC accepted CMI's Midterm Report in June 2025 — confirming the college has made meaningful progress on its core standards since the last comprehensive review.

ISER Committees — Structure & Standards Coverage
Following the ACCJC liaison visit in April 2025, CMI formed four committees to develop the Institutional Self Evaluation Report. Each committee is co-chaired by a faculty and a staff member and is responsible for gathering documentation and evidence for their respective standards area.
Standard I
Institutional Mission & Effectiveness

Covers CMI's mission statement, institutional planning, program review processes, and how the college evaluates its own effectiveness in achieving mission-driven outcomes.

Standard II
Student Success

Covers instructional programs, student support services, library and learning resources, and how CMI ensures students achieve stated learning outcomes and completion goals.

Standard III
Infrastructure & Resources

Covers human resources, physical and technology infrastructure, financial resources, and the college's capacity to sustain and improve operations in support of its mission.

Standard IV
Governance & Decision-Making

Covers board governance, administrative leadership, faculty and staff participation in shared governance, and how CMI makes decisions that reflect institutional integrity and accountability.

Nursing Programmatic Accreditation — ASEN Pathway
Target: April 2026
Initial ASEN application — programmatic accreditor for associate-level nursing programs. This begins the formal candidacy process separate from ACCJC institutional accreditation.
Key Prerequisite
New nursing faculty hired with PhD in Hospital Administration, MBA, and MSc in Nursing — a required step toward programmatic accreditation candidacy.
Long-Term Goal
ASEN candidacy → full accreditation → enables development of a Bachelor's degree in Nursing and strengthens CMI's regional healthcare training capacity.

Q3 · Agriculture Extension Activities

The Agriculture team continued its multi-pronged community engagement strategy in Q3, combining technical demonstrations with hands-on training across schools, community groups, and CMI staff — reaching over 125 participants through outreach presentations and garden activities.

10×10 Community Garden Initiative — 4 Majuro Communities
Continued technical assistance, support and maintenance to 2 clients at Batkan. Collaborating with four Majuro communities to establish new 10×10 gardens, expanding local food production capacity at the neighbourhood level.
Outreach Presentations — 125 Participants Total
9 participants at Laura High School — hands-on training (8 youth males, 1 youth female, aged 6–14)
31 participants at Arrak Community & Laura Full Gospel Youth (15 adult male, 4 adult female, 7 youth male, 5 youth female, aged 20–40)

Poultry Program — Arrak & Laura
Arrak Campus: Started with 39 chicks, expanded to 53 — currently 15 remaining. 320 eggs laid; 25 chicks donated to the community.
Laura Campus: Started with 15 mixed breeds — 146 eggs produced, 49 chicks produced.
Challenges: Lack of formula feed and inadequate staffing remain key operational constraints.
Livestock Extension Outreaches
Sustainable piggery production training with 4 Laura farmers, 25 CMI staff (15 adult males, 10 adult females), and 8 adult female MALGOV trainees.
Q3 · Aquaculture Extension Activities

The Aquaculture team focused on marine conservation and awareness in Q3, establishing coral nursery infrastructure near Laura and conducting targeted awareness sessions with youth groups and students — reinforcing the connection between healthy marine ecosystems and community food security.

Coral Replantation & Nurseries — Partnership with MICS
Continued coral replantation efforts and established coral nurseries — three cages installed near Laura in partnership with the Marshall Islands Conservation Society (MICS). This long-term marine conservation initiative supports reef health and potential future aquaculture substrate.
Giant Clam Conservation
Collecting giant clams and consolidating them at a single site to facilitate easy broadcast spawning — an important step in restoring clam populations and building toward future hatchery-based aquaculture production of this economically important species in RMI.
Community & Student Awareness
11 Full Gospel youths (Campus Boys) — community outreach and aquaculture orientation.
59 Upward Bound students (26 male youths, 33 female youths) — awareness sessions on aquaculture benefits and clam hybrid breeding techniques.

The Health and Nutrition team delivered comprehensive awareness sessions to Upward Bound students, covering foundational concepts of why nutrition matters across multiple life dimensions — from physical health to psychological well-being and social relationships.

Q3 Research Updates

Q3 Research Activities — Coconut Flour, Makmok Starch, Edible Seaweed & Pandanus

Research — Coconut Flour (Q3 Update)

The Coconut Flour research is in its final stages, having completed all core experimental work. The team is now focused on securing formal academic publication and preparing community extension materials to share findings with the broader RMI population.

Publication Pending
Awaiting final approval from the International Journal of Environment and Rural Development (IJERD) — last communication February 2026.
Extension Materials — July 2026
Reporting in progress and preparation of extension materials (pamphlets, posters & others) underway as of July 2026 for community dissemination.
Final Report — Being Compiled
Final research report currently being compiled. This will serve as the definitive documentation of findings for institutional records and future research reference.
Research — Makmok Starch (Q3 Update)

The Makmok Starch research is advancing steadily through its HACCP and food safety framework, with all critical control steps now identified and analytical testing underway. The team is transitioning from labour-intensive manual methods to kitchen appliances to improve processing efficiency and scalability.

HACCP Plan & GMP — Completed
Development of HACCP Plan and Good Manufacturing Practices completed. Critical control steps identified: grating of tubers using nylon fibers, wet sieving, air drying, and solar drying of starch.
Analytical Testing — Ongoing
Microbiological contaminant testing and chemical contaminant testing (heavy metals) currently underway — essential for food safety certification and regulatory compliance.
Equipment Upgrade — Procurement Complete
Procurement of kitchen appliances to replace selected labour-intensive processing steps completed. Quantification of labour-intensive vs. appliance-assisted steps documented for comparative analysis.
Research — Edible Seaweed (Q3 Update)

The edible seaweed research continued its community-engaged approach in Q3, combining field collection with trial production and sensory evaluation — demonstrating the potential of locally harvested seagrapes as a nutritious, culturally appropriate, and commercially viable food source for RMI communities.

Field Collection — Arrak & Laura
Collecting Seagrapes (Caulerpa racemosa) around Arrak and Laura sites — building the supply base for ongoing trial production and establishing collection protocols.
Trial Production
Trial production using seagrapes, tuna, vegetables, garlic, and chilies — testing product feasibility, preparation methods, and palatability for local market readiness.
Sensory Analysis & Awareness
Nutritional benefits awareness sessions conducted with Land Grant and other CMI staff and at two schools — building institutional and community knowledge of seaweed's dietary value.
Research — Native Pandanus Conservation (Q3 Update)

A new and significant research initiative launched in Q3 focuses on the collection and conservation of native Pandanus varieties in Majuro — addressing the urgent need to document and preserve traditional crop diversity in the Marshall Islands before it is lost to climate change, land use changes, and reduced traditional knowledge transfer.

🌿

Why Native Pandanus Matters

Pandanus (Bōb in Marshallese) is a cornerstone of traditional RMI culture, food systems, and handicrafts. The collection and conservation of native varieties is critical to protecting biodiversity, supporting food security, and preserving cultural identity in the face of climate-driven environmental change. CMI's Land Grant program plays a unique role as the institutional custodian of this research.

Q3 · UNICEF Collaboration — WASH & Nutrition Programme

In Q3, the CMI Land Grant Program formalised its partnership with UNICEF under the Invest in WASH and Nutrition for the future of RMI children programme — a multi-outcome initiative that positions CMI as a key implementing partner for community-based water safety, nutrition, and sustainable food production across the Marshall Islands. Five sites have been confirmed for programme implementation.

Programme Objectives
Water Safety & Hygiene
Conduct water quality testing and build community and school capacity on drinking water safety, water conservation, low-cost water treatment, and hygiene practices.
School & Community Gardens
Establish school and community gardens to promote sustainable food production and improved nutrition — directly connecting CMI Land Grant's agricultural extension expertise to UNICEF's community development goals.
Cooking Challenges
Organise cooking challenges that highlight the use of healthy, locally available foods — promoting dietary diversity, reducing reliance on imported processed foods, and celebrating traditional Marshallese food culture.
5 Confirmed Programme Sites

🤝

Strategic Significance

The UNICEF-CMI Land Grant partnership brings significant institutional visibility and funding leverage to the college's extension mission. By co-implementing a UN-backed programme across five RMI communities, CMI demonstrates its capacity to serve as a trusted partner for international organisations seeking to advance the SDGs in the Pacific — particularly SDG 2 (Zero Hunger), SDG 3 (Good Health), SDG 4 (Quality Education), and SDG 6 (Clean Water).

09 · OTEC Report

OTEC-ODA Project — CMI Arrak Campus

SDGs Capacity Building Project Using Ocean Thermal Energy Conversion Technologies for Energy, Water and Food · July 2026 · KRISO & CMI

KRISO × CMI Bilateral ODA Project
SDGs Capacity Building Using Ocean Thermal Energy Conversion (OTEC) Technologies for Energy, Water and Food
The OTEC-ODA project is a landmark bilateral cooperation between the Korea Research Institute of Ships & Ocean Engineering (KRISO) and the College of the Marshall Islands (CMI), aimed at transforming the CMI Arrak Campus into a sustainable green campus — a living demonstration of ocean renewable energy addressing the RMI's food, energy, and water security challenges.
Project Period
Aug 2023 – Jun 2027
Total Budget
6,600M KRW ($5.0M→$4.4M)
Location
CMI Arrak Campus, Majuro, RMI
Report Date
July 2026
Section 1 · Vision & Strategy — Korea SDGs Activity

At the heart of this project is a bold vision encapsulated in the acronym KOREA — Korea Ocean Renewable Energy Applying SDGs Activity. The initiative harnesses OTEC technology, which exploits the natural thermal gradient between warm surface seawater and cold deep ocean water, to simultaneously address multiple Sustainable Development Goals through a single integrated infrastructure at the CMI Arrak Campus.

SDG #14
Life Below Water
OTEC deep seawater intake infrastructure, environmentally monitored and permitted through RMI EPA
SDG #7
Affordable & Clean Energy
50kW OTEC pilot plant generating 250 MWh/yr of clean power — equal to CMI Arrak's full annual consumption
SDG #6
Clean Water & Sanitation
PV-RO desalination producing 6,570 m³/yr of fresh water — 50% provided free to local communities during drought emergencies
SDG #2
Zero Hunger
PV-based hydroponics system producing 24,000 heads of vegetables/yr — 150RT SWAC cooling supports aqua/agri-culture
SDG #4
Quality Education
Sustainable Seawater Utilization Academy (SSUA) trains RMI residents and CMI students in OTEC, hydroponics, desalination, and renewable energy
🌊

Why OTEC for the Marshall Islands?

The RMI's geographic location in the Pacific provides ideal OTEC conditions — a consistent 20°C+ thermal difference between surface and deep seawater. This makes OTEC not just viable, but highly strategic for a nation facing existential threats from climate change, energy dependence on imported fossil fuels, food insecurity, and freshwater scarcity. The CMI Arrak Campus becomes the demonstration hub for a technology that could one day power and sustain entire island communities across the Pacific.

Section 2 · Three Core Project Goals

The OTEC-ODA project is structured around three mutually reinforcing goals that together build a self-sustaining green campus capable of generating its own energy, producing fresh water, growing food, and training the next generation of Pacific renewable energy practitioners.

1
Design & Installation of OTEC and DOWA Demonstration Plants

The project's physical centrepiece is the construction of a 50kW OTEC pilot power generation plant alongside a suite of Discharged Ocean Water Application (DOWA) systems — including a 150RT Seawater Air Conditioning (SWAC) system for district-level cooling, a 20 t/day PV-powered Reverse Osmosis (PV-RO) desalination plant, and a PV-based hydroponics system of 100 sets. Together, these systems form an integrated Food-Energy-Water (FEW) nexus demonstration facility at the Arrak campus, capable of delivering maximum annual benefits of approximately $391,611 in energy savings, water production, vegetable yield, and CO₂ offset.

2
SSUA Training Program — Building Local Expertise in Sustainable Seawater Utilization

The Sustainable Seawater Utilization Academy (SSUA) is the project's human capital arm — designed to ensure that when KRISO transfers all facilities to CMI in June 2027, local staff have the technical skills to operate them independently. Training progresses across three annual themes: Year 2 (Hydroponics) — hands-on growing of red leaf lettuce and other crops for residents surrounding Arrak campus; Year 3 (OTEC Energy) — seawater intake, energy utilization, and OTEC operation and maintenance; Year 4 (Desalination) — PV-RO operation, water quality management, and hydroponics dissemination to neighboring schools. The programme is co-developed by KRISO and CMI, with Mr. Dako Nating (CMI) leading courses and Korean experts providing field support.

3
SDGs Capacity Building Through OTEC & DOWA Utilization at CMI Arrak Campus

Beyond the physical installations and training, this goal addresses the broader policy and community dimension: positioning the CMI Arrak Campus as a regional model for SDG achievement through ocean technology. This includes OTEC's reflection into the RMI National Energy Roadmap, socioeconomic surveys of communities west and east of Arrak campus, Environmental Impact Assessments (EIA/EmPA/EMP) fully submitted and approved by RMI EPA, and a planned community water donation programme that will provide 50% of fresh water output free of charge during drought emergencies — with the remaining 50% sold to cover ongoing system operation, maintenance, and repair costs.

OTEC Power Output
250
MWh/yr expected · equals CMI Arrak annual consumption
Fresh Water Production

m³/yr · PV-RO desalination system

heads/yr · PV hydroponics system

📌

CMI's Role & Commitment

CMI is not a passive recipient in this project — it is an active co-implementer. CMI experts lead the SSUA training curriculum, CMI coordinates community outreach and land access, and CMI will ultimately own and operate all transferred facilities from June 2027. The project directly strengthens CMI's capacity to serve as a hub for sustainable development education and technology dissemination across the Marshall Islands and the broader Pacific region. For further details on project timeline, construction scope, and challenges, please refer to the full OTEC-ODA Report (Slides 4–7).
